questions.prompt: During ion implantation, what is the job of the patterned \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) layer during ion implantation?
options: It supplies the dopant atoms that diffuse into the silicon
It converts the implanted ions into active donors
It blocks the ions everywhere except where windows have been etched, so only the openings get doped
It protects the photoresist from the UV exposure
questions.explanation: Ions are implanted over the whole wafer surface. Oxide-covered regions stop them; the etched windows let them reach the silicon. The oxide is a mask, not a dopant source; activation happens in the later high-temperature step.

questions.prompt: The substrate is already prepared. Order the making of a doped region. Each step after the first uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The oxide has to exist before the resist can record windows in it. The etch uses that record, and the implant uses the windows the etch opened. The heat is last because it moves the ions the implant just placed. Implanting before the windows exist would dope the whole surface.
steps: Grow the oxide layer that will become the implant mask.
Coat that oxide with photoresist and expose the resist through a mask, so the resist records where the windows belong.
Develop the exposed resist and etch, opening windows in the oxide where the resist was removed.
Implant through those windows, then heat the wafer so the ions that passed through the windows move onto lattice sites.

questions.prompt: Silicon has about \(5\times10^{22}\) atoms per cm³. A region is doped at \(N_D = 2\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). On average, how many silicon atoms are there per dopant atom?
questions.explanation: \[\frac{5\times10^{22}}{2\times10^{16}} = 2.5\times10^{6}\] Even a 'heavy' design doping replaces only one atom in millions, which is why the starting wafer must be purer still (about 1 part in \(10^9\)).

questions.prompt: Why must the starting wafer's unintentional impurity level be around \(10^{12}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) or lower?
options: Intentional doping goes as low as about \(10^{14}\), so stray impurities must be one to two orders of magnitude below that
Impurities above \(10^{12}\) would make silicon metallic
Photoresist cannot be exposed on impure wafers
Oxide cannot grow if impurities exceed \(10^{12}\)
questions.explanation: Designers dope from roughly \(10^{14}\) to \(10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). If the background impurities were comparable, the lightest doping levels would be uncontrolled.

questions.prompt: An implant delivers a dose of \(3\times10^{13}\) donors per cm² of surface. If the dopants end up spread uniformly through a layer \(0.6\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) deep, what is the doping concentration (in cm⁻³)?
questions.explanation: Dose is atoms per area; dividing by the depth (in cm) gives atoms per volume: \[N = \frac{3\times10^{13}}{0.6\times10^{-4}} = 5\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\] Common mistake: forgetting \(1\ \mu\mathrm{m} = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{cm}\).

questions.prompt: A positive photoresist is exposed to ultraviolet light through a mask and then developed. Exactly one step is wrong.
questions.explanation: Positive resist washes away where the light hit. The shaded resist was not changed, so it stays and protects the film underneath. A negative resist would reverse that. Exposure does not remove the oxide by itself; the etch does that after the resist has been developed.
steps: Ultraviolet light passes through the clear parts of the mask and hits the resist.
Development removes the resist that was changed.
The regions shaded by the mask are the ones that wash away.
reasons: Positive resist washes away where the ultraviolet light hit. The shaded resist stays.
Exposure hardens the whole film, so none of the resist is removed.

questions.prompt: The \(5\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) layer from before is \(0.6\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) thick with electron mobility \(250\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\,s)}\). What is its sheet resistance \(R_\square = 1/(qN\mu t)\) in Ω per square?
questions.explanation: \[R_\square = \frac{1}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(5\times10^{17})(250)(0.6\times10^{-4})} \approx 83\ \Omega/\square\] Note \(qN\mu t = q\mu Q\): the sheet resistance depends only on the dose, not on how deep it spreads.

questions.prompt: Select every property that makes silicon dioxide useful while shaping a silicon wafer.
options: It can be grown on the silicon surface.
It insulates.
It conducts well enough to replace a metal interconnect.
A thick layer of it can mask an implant.
questions.explanation: The oxide grows on the wafer, blocks current, and stops ions outside the etched windows. It is not the interconnect metal. Its permittivity is also lower than silicon's, which matters for capacitors and is not a reason to call the oxide a conductor.

questions.prompt: A wafer is polished to \(700\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) thick, but devices only use roughly the top \(2\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). What fraction (as a percentage) of the wafer thickness is the active layer?
questions.explanation: \(2/700 \approx 0.29\%\). Almost all of the wafer is mechanical support; everything happens in thin films at the top surface.

questions.prompt: Preview of IC resistors: an n-type implanted strip in a p-type substrate is used as a resistor. What condition keeps it isolated from the substrate?
options: The strip must be biased below the substrate
An oxide layer must separate the strip from the substrate
No condition: the substrate has higher resistance
The strip must never go below the substrate potential, so the n-strip/p-substrate junction stays reverse biased
questions.explanation: The strip and substrate form a pn junction. Reverse biased, it blocks DC current, leaving only a distributed capacitance to the substrate.

questions.prompt: Preview of IC resistors: a resistor strip uses the \(83\ \Omega/\square\) layer and is 40 squares long. Ignoring the contacts, what is its resistance in kΩ?
questions.explanation: \(R = R_\square \cdot (L/W) = 83.3 \times 40 \approx 3.33\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). Counting squares is how IC resistors are designed.

questions.prompt: Preview of MOSFET structure: which processing idea from this skill also forms a MOSFET's source and drain?
options: Implanting through windows defined by a mask, with the gate itself acting as part of the mask (self-aligned)
Depositing metal directly on bare silicon
Growing a thick oxide over the source and drain
Shining UV on the substrate to create carriers
questions.explanation: Source and drain are n+ regions implanted into the p body. The poly gate blocks the implant beneath it, so the source and drain line up with the gate edges automatically.
